## Working papers

### An Industry-Level Measure of Quality-Adjusted Human Capital in the European Union

*With [Juan Durán Vanegas](#) and [Iulia Siedschlag](#). ESRI Working Paper No. 812, October 2025.* \
[[Paper]](files/Duran-Jordan-Siedschlag_2025_QAHC-EU_paper.pdf){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-secondary}
[[Policy brief]](files/Duran-Jordan-Siedschlag_2025_QAHC-EU_brief.pdf){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-secondary}

This paper examines the role of human capital in driving labour-productivity growth across industries in the European Union and the United Kingdom from 2010 to 2021. Building on Égert et al. (2022), we introduce an industry-level quality-adjusted human capital (QAHC) measure that combines the quantity of education with its quality, drawing on test-score data from the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) and Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), mean years of schooling, and industry employment composition from EU KLEMS and INTANProd. Estimated within a Stochastic Frontier framework, the measure yields plausible output elasticities and is statistically associated with labour-productivity growth, particularly in goods-producing industries. These results stand in contrast to those obtained using conventional education-attainment proxies, which fail to capture a comparable productivity link.

## Theses

### The Impact of Light Rail Transit Extensions on Residential Property Prices: Evidence from Dublin's Luas Cross City Project

*Undergraduate thesis, Trinity College Dublin, April 2024. Supervisor: Ronan Lyons.* \
[[Thesis]](files/Jordan_2024_Luas-LRT_thesis.pdf){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-secondary}

This dissertation investigates the capitalisation of light rail transit (LRT) access into residential property prices, using the 2017 Luas Cross City extension in Dublin as a quasi-experimental setting. I estimate the treatment effect using hedonic pricing, difference-in-differences, and instrumental-variables designs, identifying the response of prices to distance from new stops. To mitigate endogeneity in route and station placement, I instrument for proximity to the extension with distance to Dublin's nineteenth-century historical rail network. The analysis documents a non-linear distance gradient: the DiD specification yields a 5.78% post-opening price premium within 1,000 metres of a new stop, while the IV specification estimates a 13.1% premium in the 400–800 metre band. The findings are consistent with the view that anticipated and realised transport-accessibility gains are internalised into the local housing market, and contribute to the growing quasi-experimental literature on light rail and land values.

## Works in progress

### Behavioural Responses to Housing Subsidies: Evidence from Ireland's Help to Buy Scheme

*MRes thesis, Sciences Po, 2026 (in progress).*

This paper studies how a targeted housing subsidy jointly distorts transaction values at an eligibility threshold and reshapes the composition of buyers within the treated segment. In the setting of Ireland's Help to Buy scheme — a tax-based subsidy for first-time buyers of new-build dwellings at or below €500,000, introduced at 5% in 2017 and enhanced to 10% in 2020 — I develop a developer-side notch model linking the two margins and combine it with bunching estimation and distributional and buyer-participation difference-in-differences designs, using Property Price Register data and administrative records of household purchases. I find clear excess mass just below the €500,000 threshold in the treated market under both regimes, implying a transaction-value response of roughly one-third of the maximum statutory relief, together with a pronounced shift of first-time buyer purchases towards new-builds; both margins approximately double when the marginal subsidy rate rises from 5% to 10%. The results point to an unavoidable trade-off in subsidy targeting: the design choices that direct support towards intended buyers also concentrate behavioural distortion at the eligibility boundary, and both effects intensify with subsidy generosity.
